VN.phraseNote: Pronunciation is a rough guide, following the northern accent. Vietnamese has six tones, so tap 🔊 to hear a phrase where your phone has a Vietnamese voice, or tap a phrase to show it large.

phrases.note: To be polite, add anh (to a man) or chị (to a woman) after a phrase: "Cảm ơn chị."

items.note: Useful with street sellers and drivers.
"Vâng" (vuhng) is also common in the north.

items.note: In Hà Nội you'll also hear "thanh toán" (tahn twahn).
Written "k" on signs. "Ngàn" (ngahn) in the south.
Sellers often just say "năm mươi", meaning 50k.
Point at the menu or the dish.

customs: Tipping isn't expected. Rounding up or leaving small change is appreciated; spa and massage staff often expect ₫50,000–100,000.
Bargain politely at markets and with street sellers, with a smile. Shops and cafés with printed prices are fixed.
Cover shoulders and knees at temples and pagodas, and take your shoes off where you see others' shoes at the door, including in homes.
Hand money and gifts to older people with both hands.
Don't leave chopsticks standing upright in a rice bowl; it looks like incense at a funeral.
Crossing the road: walk at a slow, steady pace and don't stop or run. Riders steer around you.
Public displays of anger cause loss of face and rarely help. Stay calm and smile when sorting out a problem.

p: Vietnam's capital for most of the last thousand years, on the Red River in the north. The Old Quarter's narrow streets, each once named for the trade carried on there, wrap around Hoàn Kiếm Lake; French-era boulevards and the Ba Đình political district lie to the west.
Hà Nội has real seasons: hot, humid summers with heavy rain, and a cool, grey winter from December to February. October and November are the best months, with dry, warm days and cooler evenings.

items.d: The heart of the city, with the red Thê Húc bridge out to Ngọc Sơn Temple on its island. Best early in the morning, when locals exercise around the shore. The fee is for the temple; the lake is free.
The tangle of streets north of the lake, each once named for the trade carried on there. Tube houses, street food and the Đồng Xuân market. Free to wander.
Văn Miếu, built in 1070 to honour Confucius and later Vietnam's first university. Five quiet courtyards and stone steles on turtles naming past scholars.
Hồ Chí Minh lies in state here. Free, mornings only, closed Mondays and Fridays and for a few weeks each year; dress code applies (see Customs). The One Pillar Pagoda is a short walk behind.
A UNESCO site: the seat of Vietnamese kings for eight centuries, with excavated palace foundations, the Đoan Môn gate and wartime bunkers.
Built by the French for Vietnamese prisoners, later the "Hanoi Hilton" for American pilots. Sobering but well presented; allow an hour.
The best museum in town: the life and crafts of Vietnam's 54 ethnic groups, with full-size village houses in the garden. A Grab ride west of the centre; closed Mondays.
Hà Nội's oldest pagoda, its tall red stupa on a small island in West Lake. Lovely at sunset. Free; cover shoulders and knees.
Beef noodle soup, the classic Hà Nội breakfast. The northern style has a clear broth and few herbs.
Grilled pork patties and belly in a sweet-sour broth, with rice noodles and herbs. A lunchtime dish.
Silky steamed rice rolls filled with pork and wood-ear mushroom, with fish sauce for dipping.
Turmeric-marinated fish fried at the table with dill and spring onion. A Hà Nội speciality.
Fried tofu, rice noodles and herbs with fermented shrimp paste. Love it or hate it.
Egg coffee: yolk whipped with condensed milk on strong coffee. Invented in Hà Nội in the 1940s.
Young green sticky rice, wrapped in lotus leaves. An autumn treat, best in September and October.
Múa rối nước: wooden puppets perform on a water stage to live chèo folk music. Thăng Long Theatre by Hoàn Kiếm Lake has several shows a day.
Centuries-old chamber singing with a long-necked lute and wooden clappers, on UNESCO's list of heritage in need of protection. Small evening shows run in the Old Quarter.
Street ballads once sung by blind wandering musicians, revived on weekend evenings near Đồng Xuân market.
From Friday to Sunday evening the roads around Hoàn Kiếm Lake close to traffic: buskers, folk games, dancing and families out late.
Fresh, light draught beer brewed daily, drunk on tiny plastic stools. Tạ Hiện street is the busiest corner.

list: At the Hồ Chí Minh Mausoleum: shoulders and knees covered, no hands in pockets, no talking or photos inside. It opens mornings only and closes on Mondays and Fridays.

items.t: Bottle of water from a shop
Iced coffee at a street stall
Grab car, airport to Old Quarter

list: The ₫20,000 and ₫500,000 notes are both blue polymer. Check before you hand one over, especially at night.
Unmetered taxis and xích lô (cyclos) that change the price at the end. Agree the total first, or use Grab.
Fruit sellers who put their shoulder pole on you for a photo, then ask for money. Shoe shiners who start before you agree.
Phones snatched from passing motorbikes. Hold yours away from the road side.
The Mausoleum closes for maintenance for about two months most years. Check before you go.

p: Vietnam's biggest city and business capital, still widely called Sài Gòn. The centre has the French-era landmarks: the Opera House, the Central Post Office, Notre-Dame Cathedral and Bến Thành market. Chợ Lớn to the west is the historic Chinese quarter, full of temples and wholesale markets.
It's hot all year, around 25–34 °C. The rainy season runs from May to November, usually as short, heavy downpours in the afternoon. The food and street life run late into the night.

items.d: Broken rice with grilled pork chop, steamed egg meatloaf and sweet fish sauce. The city's breakfast.
Noodles in a clear pork broth, from the Chinese-Vietnamese community of Chợ Lớn.
A big crispy turmeric pancake with shrimp, pork and bean sprouts, wrapped in lettuce and herbs.
Sài Gòn style is generously filled with pâté, cold cuts, pickles and chilli.
Snails and shellfish cooked a dozen ways, an evening food eaten with beer on plastic stools.
Fried rice-flour cake with egg and pickled papaya, an afternoon snack.
Strong drip coffee over ice with condensed milk. Coffee culture here is huge, from street stools to rooftop cafés.
Southern chamber music from the Mekong Delta, played on zithers and moon lutes. UNESCO-listed.
Southern 'reformed opera' mixing folk melodies with melodrama. Still performed at a few theatres and hugely popular on TV.

items.t: Bamboo circus at the Opera House
items.d: Contemporary acrobatic shows about southern life, staged most evenings in the French-era Opera House.
A wide pedestrian boulevard leading to the old City Hall, busy with families, buskers and skaters every evening.
The backpacker street: loud bars, street food and people-watching until the early hours.

list: Chợ Lớn's temples, such as Thiên Hậu, are active places of worship. Keep your voice down and step over, not on, the raised door thresholds.

items.t: Bottle of water from a shop
Iced coffee at a street stall
Beer at a bar on Bùi Viện

list: Bag and phone snatching from motorbikes is the most common crime. Keep your phone away from the kerb and wear bags across your body.
Taxis with fast meters. Use Grab, Xanh SM, or the big taxi firms Vinasun (white) and Mai Linh (green).
Overcharging at Bến Thành market. Ask a few stalls and agree the price before buying.
The ₫20,000 and ₫500,000 notes are both blue polymer. Check before you hand one over.
Streets can flood quickly in the afternoon storms of the rainy season.

p: Central Vietnam's biggest city, on the coast between the Hải Vân Pass and Hội An. It's known for the long sandy beach at Mỹ Khê, the lit-up bridges over the Hàn River, the Sơn Trà peninsula and the Marble Mountains. Modern, clean and relaxed.
The dry season is roughly February to August. From September to December it's the rainy season, with typhoon and flood risk at its highest in October and November.

items.d: Wide turmeric rice noodles in a little rich broth, with pork, shrimp, peanuts, herbs and a sesame rice cracker.
Boiled pork rolled in rice paper with herbs and cucumber, dipped in a pungent anchovy sauce.
Fish cake noodle soup with pumpkin and pineapple.
Central-style: small, crispy pancakes dipped in a peanut and pork-liver sauce.
Pick it live at the beach restaurants and pay by weight. Ask the price per kilo before it's cooked.
Cầu Rồng breathes fire, then water, at 9 pm on Saturday and Sunday nights. Watch from the riverbank.
Classical opera with painted faces and stylised battles, staged at the Nguyễn Hiển Dĩnh Theatre.
A central-coast folk singing game, part bingo, part ballad. UNESCO-listed.
The world's largest collection of sculpture from the Hindu Cham kingdoms that ruled this coast.
International teams compete over the Hàn River on summer weekends, usually June and July.

items.t: Grab car, airport to Mỹ Khê beach
Bà Nà Hills cable car ticket

list: October and November bring typhoons and floods. Check the forecast; boat trips, hill trips and flights can be cancelled.
Strong currents at Mỹ Khê in rough weather. Swim between the lifeguard flags.
Seafood priced by weight: confirm the price per kilo and see it weighed before it's cooked.
Bà Nà Hills is high and often foggy and cold. Take a layer.

p: A small, beautifully preserved trading port on the Thu Bồn River, about 30 km south of Đà Nẵng. Its old town of ochre shophouses, Chinese assembly halls and the Japanese Covered Bridge (on the ₫20,000 note) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Silk lanterns light the streets every evening.
Beaches at An Bàng and Cửa Đại are a short bike ride away. October and November are flood season, when the riverside streets can go under water.

items.d: Chewy, smoky noodles with pork, greens and crunchy croutons. Traditionally only made in Hội An.
Turmeric chicken rice with shredded chicken, herbs and pickled onion.
Hội An's are famous; the best-known stalls have queues all day.
Bánh bao bánh vạc: translucent shrimp dumplings shaped like roses, made by one family for the whole town.
Fried wontons topped with a sweet-sour tomato and shrimp salsa.
The region's turmeric noodles, with a little broth, pork, shrimp and peanuts.
A folk singing-and-bingo game, UNESCO-listed, performed by the river in the old town most evenings. Buy a card and join in.
On the 14th day of each lunar month the old town turns down its electric lights; lanterns, music and candles float on the river.
Short traditional shows run several times a day in the old town, included with the old town ticket.
Hội An is famous for made-to-measure clothes and shoes, made in a day or two.
Small boats on the Thu Bồn after dark, where you can float a paper lantern for luck.

list: The old town is a lived-in neighbourhood. Ask before photographing people up close, and keep shoulders covered in the assembly halls.

items.t: Grab car to Đà Nẵng airport

list: Floods in October and November: Bạch Đằng and Nguyễn Thái Học streets by the river can flood, and boats replace bikes.
Tailors: allow two or three days and at least two fittings. Agree the fabric and price in writing.
Lantern boat touts may quote per person when you assumed per boat, or the reverse. Clarify first.
Buy the old town ticket at the official booths; it's checked at the entrances.

p: Vietnam's imperial capital from 1802 to 1945 under the Nguyễn dynasty, on the Perfume River (sông Hương). The walled Citadel and Imperial City, the royal tombs in the hills along the river and Thiên Mụ pagoda are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Huế is quieter and more traditional than the big cities, and its cooking, once made for the royal court, is the spiciest in Vietnam. It's also the wettest city in the country: October and November bring heavy rain and frequent floods.

items.d: Spicy lemongrass beef noodle soup with pork knuckle and congealed blood. Huế's signature dish.
Rice with tiny river clams, peanuts, pork crackling, herbs and chilli.
Steamed rice cakes: bèo are little saucers with shrimp, nậm are flat parcels in banana leaf, lọc are chewy tapioca with shrimp and pork.
Huế's crispy pancake, served with a thick peanut and pork-liver sauce.
Sweet soups and puddings; Huế has dozens of kinds, from lotus seed to taro.
Royal court music, Vietnam's first UNESCO intangible heritage. Performed at the Duyệt Thị Đường royal theatre inside the Imperial City.
Folk songs sung on a dragon boat on the Perfume River at night, ending with floating candle lanterns.
Each emperor designed his own tomb as a garden retreat; Tự Đức's, Minh Mạng's and Khải Định's are the best known.
A big arts festival with court music, processions and lantern events. Check dates, as the programme changes each year.

list: Floods in October and November can close roads to the tombs. Check before setting out.
Dragon boats to Thiên Mụ pagoda may add stops at shops. Agree the route and price first.
Food is spicy here. Say "không cay" (khom kai) for not spicy.
